attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: He names a cause (chatbots) and a mechanism (configurable pseudo-conversation). The video-game aside is commentary and is correctly kept as a qualifier. The statement is unhedged, and 'people' is left unquantified, as he wrote it.

contract.note: Reading 'insane' as causing or worsening serious delusions or psychiatric crises in some users is an ordinary reading of colloquial language, and it does not require any prevalence. The result depends on what causal standard is applied, which the speaker did not supply.

evidence.note: Published June 10, 2025, inside the target period. A psychiatrist reviewed screenshots and said the bots were worsening delusions. This points toward the claim, but it lacks clinical histories and any check of other causes, so it does not meet the support condition.
April 2025 preprint showing that chatbots validate delusional prompts. That makes the mechanism plausible but measures no patient outcomes.
July 2025 commentary by a psychiatrist calling the causal question open. It shows the uncertainty but does not disprove harm.

reviews.rationale: The packet has contemporaneous reports and a psychiatrist's view that chatbots worsened delusions, plus a plausible mechanism. It has no clinical case histories or studies that rule out other causes, which the support condition requires, and no strong evidence against the claim. The evidence does not settle it either way.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words, rebutting Roose's piece in his own voice.

semantics.note: An unhedged claim about the evidence record that existed by June 2025. 'This' is ambiguous: it could mean Roose's two trends or AI displacing entry-level jobs generally. The drafter ties it to the piece without choosing.

contract.note: The contract narrows 'this' to Roose's two specific employer practices. That is a plausible nearest-referent reading but not the only one. Under the broader reading, data on entry-level hiring declines would count, so the referent choice drives the result.

evidence.note: Published May 2025, before the post. It documents weaker hiring of new graduates and mentions AI among possible causes, but leans toward funding conditions. It does not document premature AI substitution or AI-driven cuts to training.

reviews.rationale: The search did not find a pre-publication source documenting either practice, but a limited search cannot establish that no proof existed. The one item is context only. Under the contract, the evidence neither confirms the absence of proof nor contradicts it.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words, written in his own voice.

semantics.note: A two-part observation (some advantages; far from a panacea), captured faithfully. 'Some' is preserved.

contract.note: Plain reading: practical benefits for some engineers, with substantial limits remaining. This is a fair, ordinary reading, and the March to June 2025 target period fits his present-tense claim.

evidence.note: Atlassian survey fielded in March 2025, published in July. Developers reported AI time savings while losing similar time to friction that AI did not fix. Atlassian sells developer tools, so this is a company disclosure, but it fits both parts of the claim.

METR randomized trial run February to June 2025: experienced developers were slowed down despite perceiving a speedup. This strengthens 'far from a panacea' and qualifies measured advantages. Its window extends past the post date.

reviews.rationale: Survey evidence from the target period shows developers reporting real benefits from AI tools while major workflow problems remained. The METR study adds that perceived gains may overstate measured ones, which reinforces 'far from a panacea'. Nothing in the packet shows the advantages were absent or that the tools solved engineering problems wholesale.
